slides.title: Unit 1: Theory of Consumer Behavior
content: Introduction to Consumer Behavior
A consumer is a decision-making unit (individual or household) who uses or consumes goods/services.
Theory focuses on how a consumer decides on the basket of goods/services to maximize satisfaction.
Key assumptions: Limited income, Rationality, and Perfect information.

slides.title: 1.1 The Concept of Utility
content: Utility is the level of satisfaction or pleasure derived from the consumption of a good or service.
It is the power of a commodity to satisfy human wants.
Example: Bread satisfies hunger; water quenches thirst.

slides.title: Relativity of Utility
content: Utility is subjective and not absolute (objectively determined).
The same commodity provides different utilities to different consumers.
Example: Non-smokers derive no utility from cigarettes.
Utility varies from unit to unit, time to time, and place to place.
Example: Utility from tea in the morning is different from utility at lunch.
Utility and usefulness are not synonymous: Usefulness is a product concern; Utility is a consumer concern.

slides.title: Approaches to Measuring Utility
content: Cardinal Utility Approach: Utility is measurable quantitatively in units called 'utils' or in monetary terms.
Ordinal Utility Approach: Utility cannot be measured absolutely; it can only be ranked or ordered.
Activity: Why do you buy goods and services? Think about the utility you derive from them.

slides.title: 1.2 The Cardinal Utility Theory
content: According to this theory, utility is measurable like height, weight, or temperature.
Unit of measurement for utility is called 'utils'.
Utility can also be measured in monetary units (the amount a consumer is willing to pay).

slides.title: Assumptions of Cardinal Utility Theory
content: Rational Consumer: Consumers aim to maximize satisfaction given limited income.
Cardinal Utility: Utility is measurable.
Constant Marginal Utility of Money: The utility from each successive unit of money income is constant.
Diminishing Marginal Utility: Utility gained from successive units of a commodity diminishes.

slides.title: Measurement of Utility
content: Total Utility (TU): The total amount of satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a specific quantity of a commodity (X).
TU increases as consumption increases, but eventually reaches a saturation point.
Marginal Utility (MU): The additional utility obtained from consuming one more unit of a commodity.
MU = ΔTU / ΔQ
Example: If total utility increases from 10 utils to 12 utils by consuming one more orange, MU = 2 utils.

slides.title: Numerical Example: TU and MU
content: Table: Consumption of Banana
MU of the 3rd unit of banana is 7 utils.

slides.title: Relationship Between TU and MU
content: TU increases as long as MU is positive.
TU reaches maximum when MU is zero (saturation point).
TU decreases when MU becomes negative.
Graphical representation shows a downward-sloping MU curve and an inverted U-shaped TU curve.

slides.title: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility (LDMU)
content: The law states that as a consumer consumes more units of a good, the utility derived from each successive unit decreases.
Important assumptions: All other goods remain constant; consumption is over a specific time period.
Example: First glass of water provides high utility; second glass provides lower utility; the fifth glass may provide negative utility.

slides.title: 1.3 The Consumer Maximization Problem
content: A consumer maximizes utility by allocating income to different goods.
Consumer Budget Equation: Income (I) = Px × Qx + Py × Qy + ... + Pn × Qn
Key Assumptions: Rationality, Cardinal utility, Constant marginal utility of money, Diminishing marginal utility, Fixed income, Fixed prices.

slides.title: Consumer Equilibrium: One Commodity
content: Equilibrium occurs when marginal utility of the commodity equals its price.
MUx = Px
If MUx > Px: Consumer can increase welfare by buying more of the good.
If MUx < Px: Consumer can increase welfare by buying less of the good.
The equilibrium point also derives the demand curve.

slides.title: Consumer Equilibrium: More Than One Commodity
content: Equilibrium condition: MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb = ... = MUn/Pn = MUm
This means the utility derived from spending an additional birr on each commodity is equal.
If MUa/Pa > MUb/Pb, the consumer should spend more on good A.
If MUa/Pa < MUb/Pb, the consumer should spend more on good B.

slides.title: Numerical Example: Two Commodities
content: Income = Birr 22. Prices: Px = Birr 2, Py = Birr 4.
Equilibrium occurs at 3 units of X (bread) and 4 units of Y (injera).
MUx/Px = MUy/Py = 1
Maximum total utility is achieved at this combination.

slides.title: Example: Utility Maximization Table
content: Table: Utility schedules for bread (X) and injera (Y)
Quantity of X: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7
Quantity of Y: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7
Consumer equilibrium when 3 units of X and 4 units of Y are consumed.

sections.section_title: Introduction to the Ordinal Utility Theory

slides.title: 1.4 Introduction to the Ordinal Utility Theory
content: Utility cannot be measured absolutely; it can only be ranked according to preferences.
Consumers can order their preferences: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.
The concept is based on the idea that consumers can tell which bundle they prefer, but not 'how much' more.
Example: You may prefer orange over banana, but you can't say how many 'utils' more.

slides.title: Assumptions of Ordinal Utility Theory
content: Rationality: Consumer aims to maximize satisfaction given income and prices.
Utility is ordinal: Utility can only be ranked, not measured.
Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution (DMRS): Consumers are willing to give up fewer units of one good to get more of another.
Consistency: If A > B, then B is not > A.
Transitivity: If A > B and B > C, then A > C.

slides.title: Comparing Cardinal and Ordinal Utility
content: Cardinal Utility: Utility is measurable; uses 'utils'; assumptions include DMU.
Ordinal Utility: Utility is not measurable; only rankings are possible; uses DMRS.
Both assume rationality of the consumer.
Ordinal utility approach is more practical and widely used in modern economics.

slides.title: Unit 2: Theories of Demand and Supply
content: Market is where buyers and sellers interact to determine price and quantity.
Prices are determined by the interaction of demand and supply.
Key objectives: Explain theory of demand and supply, market equilibrium, and elasticity.

slides.title: 2.1 Theory of Demand
content: Demand is the ability and willingness to buy a specific quantity of a commodity at a given price in a given period.
Demand = Willingness to buy + Ability to pay.
It is different from a desire or want, which may not be backed by purchasing power.

slides.title: Demand Schedule, Function, and Curve
content: Demand Schedule: A table showing quantities demanded at different prices.
Demand Function: Qd = f(P) = a - bP, where Qd is quantity demanded, P is price.
Demand Curve: A graphical representation; Price on Y-axis, Quantity on X-axis.
Law of Demand: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.
Reasons: Income effect, Substitution effect, and Diminishing marginal utility.

slides.title: Factors Affecting Demand
content: Price of the good (inverse relationship).
Price of related goods: Substitutes (positive relationship) and Complements (negative relationship).
Consumer income: Normal goods (positive), Inferior goods (negative).
Tastes, habits, and preferences.
Population size (larger population = higher demand).
Season (demand changes with weather).
Future price expectations (higher expected price = higher current demand).

slides.title: Change in Quantity Demanded vs Change in Demand
content: Change in Quantity Demanded: Movement along the demand curve caused by a change in the good's own price.
Extension of demand: Downward movement (price decreases, quantity increases).
Contraction of demand: Upward movement (price increases, quantity decreases).
Change in Demand: Shift of the demand curve caused by factors other than price.
Increase in demand: Shift to the right (outward).
Decrease in demand: Shift to the left (inward).

slides.title: Derivation of Market Demand
content: Individual Demand: Quantity a single person is willing and able to buy at a given price.
Market Demand: Total quantity all consumers are willing and able to buy.
Market demand is obtained by horizontally summing individual demand curves.
Example: If Qd_individual = 50 - 5P and there are 100 identical buyers, then Qd_market = 100 × (50 - 5P) = 5000 - 500P.

slides.title: 2.2 Theory of Supply
content: Supply: The various amounts of a product that a producer is willing and able to produce and sell at a given price.
Sellers constitute the supply side of the market.
Ceteris Paribus: Holding other factors constant, quantity supplied is the amount offered for sale at a given price.

slides.title: Supply Function, Schedule, and Curve
content: Supply Function: Qs = f(P) = a + bP, where Qs is quantity supplied, P is price.
Supply Schedule: A table showing quantities supplied at different prices.
Supply Curve: Graphical representation; upward sloping.
Law of Supply: Price and quantity supplied are directly related.
A supplier needs a minimum price to start supplying, then increases quantity as price rises.

slides.title: Change in Quantity Supplied vs Change in Supply
content: Change in Quantity Supplied: Movement along the supply curve caused by a change in the good's own price.
Change in Supply: Shift of the supply curve caused by factors other than price.
Factors causing shift in supply:
- Input prices
- Technology
- Taxes and subsidies
- Number of sellers
- Expectations
- External factors (e.g., weather).

slides.title: Derivation of Market Supply
content: Individual Supply: Quantity a single producer is willing to sell at a given price.
Market Supply: Total quantity all producers are willing to sell.
Market supply is obtained by horizontally summing individual supply curves.
Example: If Qs_individual = 20P - 5 and there are 120 identical sellers, then Qs_market = 120 × (20P - 5) = 2400P - 600.
When P = 4, Qs_market = 2400(4) - 600 = 9,000 tons.

slides.title: 2.3 Market Equilibrium
content: Market Equilibrium: A state where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Equilibrium Price (Market Clearing Price): The price at which Qd = Qs.
Equilibrium Quantity: The quantity bought and sold at equilibrium price.
At equilibrium, there is no tendency for price to change.

slides.title: Market Equilibrium: Numerical Example
content: Demand (units): 4 | 3 | 2
Supply (units): 2 | 3 | 4
Market Position: Shortage (-) | Equilibrium | Surplus (+)
Equilibrium at Price = 20 and Quantity = 3 units.

slides.title: Excess Demand and Excess Supply
content: Excess Demand (Shortage): Qd > Qs. Occurs when price is below equilibrium.
Result: Consumers bid the price up.
Excess Supply (Surplus): Qs > Qd. Occurs when price is above equilibrium.
Result: Producers bid the price down.
Market forces always push towards equilibrium.

slides.title: Effects of Changes in Demand and Supply
content: Change in Demand (Supply Constant):
- Increase in demand → Equilibrium price ↑, Equilibrium quantity ↑.
- Decrease in demand → Equilibrium price ↓, Equilibrium quantity ↓.
Change in Supply (Demand Constant):
- Increase in supply → Equilibrium price ↓, Equilibrium quantity ↑.
- Decrease in supply → Equilibrium price ↑, Equilibrium quantity ↓.
When both shift, the effect on price and quantity depends on the direction and magnitude of the shifts.

slides.title: Factors Shifting Demand and Supply
content: Factors shifting Demand (Supply constant):
- Income (increase → demand ↑, decrease → demand ↓)
- Substitutes (increase in price of substitute → demand ↑)
- Complements (increase in price of complement → demand ↓)
- Tastes and preferences (favorable → demand ↑)
- Number of consumers (increase → demand ↑)
Factors shifting Supply (Demand constant):
- Resource prices (increase → supply ↓)
- Technology (improvement → supply ↑)
- Taxes (increase → supply ↓)
- Subsidies (increase → supply ↑)
- Number of suppliers (increase → supply ↑)

slides.title: 2.4 Elasticities of Demand and Supply
content: Elasticity: A measure of the sensitivity of one variable to another.
It tells us the percentage change in one variable in response to a 1% change in another variable.
Types of Demand Elasticities:
1. Price Elasticity of Demand
2. Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
3. Income Elasticity of Demand
Also: Price Elasticity of Supply.

slides.title: Price Elasticity of Demand
content: Price Elasticity of Demand (Ed): Measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.
Ed = Percentage change in quantity demanded / Percentage change in price
Point Elasticity: Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q)
Arc Elasticity: Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P1+P2)/(Q1+Q2)
Since price and quantity demanded are inversely related, Ed is usually negative. We use the absolute value.
Interpretation:
- If |Ed| > 1: Elastic (demand is responsive to price changes).
- If |Ed| < 1: Inelastic (demand is not very responsive to price changes).
- If |Ed| = 1: Unitary elastic (proportional response).

slides.title: Examples and Special Cases of Elasticity
content: Perfectly Inelastic: |Ed| = 0. Quantity demanded does not change when price changes.
Example: Life-saving medicine.
Perfectly Elastic: |Ed| = ∞. Consumers will buy all they can at a given price, nothing at a higher price.
Example: Perfectly competitive market.
Determinants of Price Elasticity:
- Availability of substitutes
- Nature of the good (necessity vs luxury)
- Proportion of income spent on the good
- Time horizon (more elastic in the long run)

slides.title: Cross Elasticity of Demand
content: Cross Elasticity (Exy): Measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded of good X to a change in the price of good Y.
Exy = Percentage change in quantity demanded of X / Percentage change in price of Y
Interpretation:
- Positive Exy: Goods are substitutes (e.g., coffee and tea).
- Negative Exy: Goods are complements (e.g., cars and petrol).
- Zero Exy: Goods are independent (unrelated).

slides.title: Income Elasticity of Demand
content: Income Elasticity (Ei): Measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in consumer income.
Ei = Percentage change in quantity demanded / Percentage change in income
Interpretation:
- Positive Ei: Normal good. Demand increases as income increases.
- Ei > 1: Luxury good (demand increases more than proportionally).
- 0 < Ei < 1: Necessity good (demand increases less than proportionally).
- Negative Ei: Inferior good. Demand decreases as income increases.

slides.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
content: Price Elasticity of Supply (Es): Measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price.
Es = Percentage change in quantity supplied / Percentage change in price
Point Elasticity: Es = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q)
Arc Elasticity: Es = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P1+P2)/(Q1+Q2)
Since price and quantity supplied are directly related, Es is positive.
Interpretation:
- If Es > 1: Supply is elastic.
- If Es < 1: Supply is inelastic.
- If Es = 1: Supply is unitary elastic.
Determinants: Time, availability of inputs, number of sellers.

slides.title: Unit 3: Theories of Production and Cost
content: This unit examines the behavior of firms in producing goods and services.
Production involves transforming inputs into outputs.
Cost is the expenditure incurred to acquire inputs.
The unit covers production functions, cost curves, and their relationships.

slides.title: 3.1 Theory of Production
content: Production: The process of transforming inputs (raw materials, labor, capital) into desired outputs (goods/services).
Production Function: A function showing the maximum output a firm can produce with a given combination of inputs.
Q = f(L, K), where L = Labor, K = Capital.
Short-run: At least one factor of production is fixed.
Long-run: All factors of production are variable.

slides.title: Short Run Production Function
content: Short-run: Capital (K) is fixed, Labor (L) is variable.
Q = f(L, K̄) where K̄ is fixed.
Key Concepts:
- Total Product (TP): Total output produced.
- Average Product (AP): TP per unit of variable input. APL = TP/L.
- Marginal Product (MP): Additional output from one more unit of variable input. MPL = ΔTP/ΔL.

slides.title: Law of Diminishing Marginal Productivity
content: The law states that as more of a variable input is added to a fixed input, the marginal product of the variable input will eventually decline.
Example: Adding more workers to a fixed amount of land.
Initially, MP increases due to specialization.
Eventually, MP decreases because the fixed input becomes crowded.
This law explains the shape of the TP curve (increasing at a decreasing rate).

slides.title: Stages of Production
content: Stage I (Increasing Returns): MP is rising and positive. AP is increasing.
Stage II (Diminishing Returns): MP is positive but decreasing. AP is decreasing.
This is the rational stage of production.
Stage III (Negative Returns): MP is negative. TP is decreasing.
A rational firm will not operate in Stage III.

slides.title: Numerical Example: Short Run Production
content: Fixed input: 1 hectare of land
Stage I: L=1 to L=4 (MP increasing)
Stage II: L=5 to L=11 (MP positive but decreasing)
Stage III: L=12+ (MP negative)

slides.title: Long Run Production Function: Isoquants
content: In the long run, all inputs are variable.
Isoquant: A curve showing all combinations of two inputs that produce the same level of output.
Example: Combinations of Labor and Capital to produce 100 units.
Properties of Isoquants:
1. Downward sloping.
2. Further from origin = Higher output.
3. Do not cross.
4. Convex to the origin.

slides.title: Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS)
content: MRTS: The rate at which one input can be substituted for another while keeping output constant.
MRTS = - ΔK / ΔL
It equals the slope of the isoquant.
Property: MRTS diminishes as we move down along an isoquant.
This is the Diminishing Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution.
It makes the isoquant convex to the origin.

slides.title: Returns to Scale
content: Returns to scale: The effect on output when all inputs are increased by the same proportion.
Types:
1. Increasing Returns to Scale: Output increases by more than the increase in inputs (m > 1).
2. Constant Returns to Scale: Output increases by the same proportion as inputs (m = 1).
3. Decreasing Returns to Scale: Output increases by less than the increase in inputs (m < 1).
Reasons: Economies/diseconomies of scale, specialization, managerial difficulties.

slides.title: Technological Change and Production Curves
content: Technological change increases the productivity of factors.
Effect on production:
- Production function shifts upward (more output from the same inputs).
- Isoquant map shifts inward (same output with fewer inputs).
Types of Technical Progress:
1. Capital-saving (Labor-using): MP_L increases more than MP_K.
2. Labor-saving (Capital-using): MP_K increases more than MP_L.
3. Neutral: Both MP_L and MP_K increase by the same proportion.

slides.title: 3.2 Theory of Cost
content: Cost of Production: The expenditure incurred on inputs to produce goods/services.
Cost function is derived from the production function.
Short-run costs: Some inputs are fixed.
Long-run costs: All inputs are variable.

slides.title: Short-Run Costs: Total Costs
content: Total Fixed Cost (TFC): Costs that do not vary with output (e.g., rent, insurance).
Total Variable Cost (TVC): Costs that vary directly with output (e.g., raw materials, wages).
Total Cost (TC) = TFC + TVC

slides.title: Short-Run Costs: Average and Marginal Costs
content: Average Fixed Cost (AFC) = TFC / Q
Average Variable Cost (AVC) = TVC / Q
Average Total Cost (ATC) = TC / Q = AFC + AVC
Marginal Cost (MC) = ΔTC / ΔQ = ΔTVC / ΔQ (since ΔTFC = 0)

slides.title: Relationship Between Cost Curves
content: AFC continuously declines as output increases.
AVC is U-shaped (decreases then increases due to law of diminishing returns).
ATC is U-shaped and lies above AVC (difference is AFC).
MC is U-shaped and intersects AVC and ATC at their minimum points.
When MC < AVC (or ATC), the curves are falling.
When MC = AVC (or ATC), the curves are at their minimum.
When MC > AVC (or ATC), the curves are rising.

slides.title: Long-Run Costs
content: In the long run, all inputs are variable, so there are no fixed costs.
Long-Run Total Cost (LTC): Cost of producing output with all inputs variable.
Long-Run Average Cost (LAC): LTC / Q.
Long-Run Marginal Cost (LMC): ΔLTC / ΔQ.
LAC curve is U-shaped, but flatter than short-run cost curves.
Economies of Scale: Downward-sloping portion of LAC (costs fall as output increases).
Diseconomies of Scale: Upward-sloping portion of LAC (costs rise as output increases).

slides.title: Relationship Between Production and Cost Curves
content: Production and cost curves are mirror images.
When AP rises → AVC falls.
When AP falls → AVC rises.
When AP is maximum → AVC is minimum.
When MP rises → MC falls.
When MP falls → MC rises.
When MP is maximum → MC is minimum.

slides.title: Unit 4: Market Structure
content: Markets are categorized based on competition levels and nature.
Types of markets: Perfectly Competitive, Monopoly, Oligopoly, Monopolistic Competition.
We analyze demand, revenue, and equilibrium in each market.

slides.title: 4.1 Perfectly Competitive Markets
content: Perfect Competition: A market with many buyers and sellers, where no single firm has market power.
Firms are price takers.
Products are identical (homogeneous).
Free entry and exit.
Perfect information.

slides.title: Characteristics of Perfect Competition
content: Large number of buyers and sellers: Each firm is too small to influence price.
Homogeneous product: Products are identical and perfect substitutes.
Free entry and exit: No barriers to entry or exit.
Perfect information: Consumers and producers have full knowledge of market conditions.
Profit maximization: The goal of every firm.

slides.title: Demand in Perfect Competition
content: A competitive firm faces a perfectly horizontal (elastic) demand curve.
It can sell any quantity at the prevailing market price.
The firm's demand curve is a horizontal line at P*.
P* is determined by the intersection of market demand and supply.

slides.title: Revenue in Perfect Competition
content: Total Revenue (TR) = P × Q
Average Revenue (AR) = TR / Q = P
Marginal Revenue (MR) = ΔTR / ΔQ = P
In perfect competition, P = AR = MR.
The AR and MR curves are the same horizontal line at the market price.

slides.title: 4.2 Pure Monopoly Market
content: Monopoly: A market structure with a single seller.
The firm and the industry are one and the same.
The product has no close substitutes.
There are high barriers to entry.
The monopolist is a price maker.

slides.title: Characteristics of Monopoly
content: Single seller and many buyers.
No close substitutes.
Price maker: The monopolist controls price by controlling supply.
Price discrimination: Selling the same product at different prices to different consumers.
Restrictions on entry: Barriers to entry exist.

slides.title: Sources of Monopoly Power
content: Absence of close substitutes.
Economies of scale: Large firms can produce at lower average cost.
Ownership of strategic inputs (e.g., mineral water).
Patent rights: Legal protection for inventions.
Government policies (licensing, trade restrictions).

slides.title: Demand in Monopoly
content: A monopolist faces the market demand curve, which is downward-sloping.
To sell more output, the monopolist must lower the price.
If the monopolist raises price, quantity demanded decreases.
The demand curve is P = a - bQ.

slides.title: Revenue in Monopoly
content: TR = P × Q = (a - bQ) × Q = aQ - bQ²
AR = TR / Q = P = a - bQ (downward-sloping).
MR = ΔTR / ΔQ = a - 2bQ (downward-sloping and lies below AR).
TR curve is an inverted U-shape: increases, reaches maximum, then decreases.
MR becomes zero at the maximum point of TR and negative afterwards.

slides.title: Monopoly: Numerical Example
content: Table: Quantity (Q) | Price (P) | TR | AR | MR
TR max at Q=5, MR becomes zero at Q=6.

slides.title: 4.3 Monopolistically Competitive Market
content: Monopolistic Competition: A market with many sellers selling differentiated products.
Free entry and exit exist.
Firms have some market power due to product differentiation.
It combines features of both perfect competition and monopoly.

slides.title: Characteristics of Monopolistic Competition
content: Product differentiation: Products are slightly different (brand, quality, style).
Many sellers and buyers: More than perfect competition, but still many.
Free entry and exit: No significant barriers.
Non-price competition: Advertising, branding, customer service are important.

slides.title: Demand and Revenue in Monopolistic Competition
content: Firms are price makers, facing a downward-sloping demand curve.
Because of many close substitutes, the demand curve is relatively elastic (flatter than monopoly).
AR (demand) and MR curves are both downward-sloping.
MR lies below AR, similar to monopoly.

slides.title: 4.4 Oligopoly Market
content: Oligopoly: A market with a few dominant firms.
Firms are mutually interdependent.
Products can be homogeneous (e.g., cement) or differentiated (e.g., cars).
There are significant barriers to entry.
Example: The world crude oil market.

slides.title: Characteristics of Oligopoly
content: Few dominant firms: Market is concentrated.
Interdependence: Each firm's decisions affect and are affected by rivals.
Barriers to entry: Economies of scale, patents, high capital requirements.
Products: Can be homogeneous or differentiated.

slides.title: Demand and Revenue in Oligopoly
content: The demand curve for an oligopolist is downward-sloping.
The shape is complex because it depends on rivals' reactions.
If a firm lowers price, rivals may follow, leading to inelastic demand.
If a firm raises price, rivals may not follow, leading to elastic demand.
AR and MR curves are downward-sloping but may be kinked (in the kinked demand curve model).

slides.title: Summary of Market Structures
content: Perfect Competition: Many firms, homogeneous product, free entry, price takers.
Monopoly: One firm, unique product, entry barriers, price maker.
Monopolistic Competition: Many firms, differentiated product, free entry, non-price competition.
Oligopoly: Few firms, homogeneous or differentiated product, entry barriers, interdependence.

slides.title: Unit 5: Banking and Finance
content: Capital is a key factor of production.
Banks transfer finance from savers to borrowers.
This unit covers financial intermediaries, markets, institutions, and Ethiopian banking history.
Indigenous financial institutions like Iqub and Iddir are also discussed.

slides.title: 5.1 Financial Intermediaries
content: Financial Intermediary: An entity that acts as a middleman between savers and borrowers.
Examples: Banks, Microfinance Institutions.
Financial Intermediation: The process of transferring funds from surplus spending units to deficit spending units.
Finance is the lifeblood of the economy.

slides.title: Benefits of Financial Intermediaries
content: For Depositors (Savers):
- Safety: Money is protected from risk of loss.
- Interest earning: Banks pay interest on savings.
For Borrowers:
- Access to capital for investment.
- Enables production, which is useful for the economy.

slides.title: 5.2 Financial Markets
content: Financial Markets: Channels for allocating savings to investment.
They provide assets to savers and funding forms for investors.
Components of Financial Markets:
1. Money Market: Short-term instruments (maturity ≤ 1 year).
2. Capital Market: Long-term instruments.

slides.title: Money Market Instruments
content: Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Issued by governments, short-term.
Commercial Papers: Short-term unsecured promissory notes issued by corporations.
Negotiable Certificates of Deposit (CDs): Time deposits with a bank.
Repurchase Agreements (Repos): Short-term borrowing.
Bankers' Acceptances: Time drafts drawn on and accepted by a bank.

slides.title: 5.3 Financial Institutions
content: Institutions: The rules of the game in society.
Formal Institutions: Written rules (constitutions, laws, policies).
Informal Institutions: Unwritten norms, customs, traditions.
Financial Institutions: Organizations that serve as financial intermediaries.

slides.title: Types of Financial Institutions
content: 1. Depository Institutions: Accept and manage deposits, make loans.
Examples: Banks, Credit Unions.
2. Contractual Institutions: Insurance companies, pension funds.
3. Investment Institutes: Investment banks, brokerage firms.

slides.title: Banking Financial Institutions
content: A bank gives loans to borrowers and accepts deposits from savers.
Roles of Banks:
- Mobilizing savings.
- Identifying good investments.
- Improving capital allocation and corporate governance.
- Managing risk and enhancing economic growth.
Efficiency depends on: Competition among banks and the nature of regulation.

slides.title: Non-Banking Financial Institutions (NBFIs)
content: NBFI: A financial institution that does not have a full banking license.
They facilitate bank-related financial services.
Examples:
- Insurance companies
- Pawn shops
- Check-cashing locations
- Payday lending
- Microloan organizations.

sections.section_title: Historical Development of Banks in Ethiopia

slides.title: 5.4 Historical Development of Banks in Ethiopia
content: Modern banking started in 1905 with the Bank of Abyssinia.
1906: Bank of Abyssinia officially founded.
1931: Replaced by the Bank of Ethiopia (state-owned).
1936-1941: Italian banks operated during occupation.
1943: State Bank of Ethiopia established (central and commercial bank).
1963: National Bank of Ethiopia (central bank) and Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE) established.

slides.title: Banking History (1974-1991)
content: Socialist period: Banks were nationalized.
Addis Bank formed from private banks.
1980: Addis Bank and CBE merged into one commercial bank.
Agricultural and Industrial Development Bank (AIDB) established.
Financial sector had only 3 banks.

slides.title: Banking History (1991-Present)
content: Shift to a liberal economy in 1991.
1994: Licensing and Supervision of Banking Business proclamation.
Allowed for private commercial banks.
Current banks: National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE), Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE), Development Bank of Ethiopia (DBE), and private banks.

slides.title: Roles of Banks in Ethiopia
content: National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE):
- Prints currency, mints coins.
- Issues bonds and treasury bills.
- Maintains low inflation.
- Authorizes and controls financial institutions.
- Lends to commercial banks.
- Regulates money supply and foreign exchange.
Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE):
- Accepts deposits.
- Gives loans.
- Handles foreign currency.
- Largest commercial bank in Ethiopia.
Development Bank of Ethiopia (DBE):
- Provides short, medium, and long-term development loans.
- Focuses on agriculture and industry projects.

slides.title: 5.5 Micro-finance Institutions
content: Microfinance provides financial services to the poor.
Founded by Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank.
Provides microcredit to economically active poor.
Microcredit: Small loans without collateral.

slides.title: Microfinance and Microcredit
content: MFIs give access to savings, credit, insurance, and money transfer.
Microcredit is a small loan given without collateral.
Group Lending: A mechanism where a group gets a loan, and peer pressure ensures repayment.
Clients: Economically active poor with entrepreneurial skills.

slides.title: Microfinance vs Money Lenders
content: Informal money lenders charge very high interest.
Borrowers have no protection from abusive practices.
Positive features of moneylenders: Simple procedures, clear terms, timely disbursement.
MFIs combine these positive features and formalize them.

slides.title: Microfinance Institutions in Ethiopia
content: As of 2020/21, there are 41 operational MFIs.
They mobilized Birr 47 billion in savings.
They provided loans worth Birr 64.6 billion.
They serve the economically active poor.

slides.title: 5.6 Electronic Banking (e-banking)
content: E-banking (EFT): Transfer of funds through electronic methods.
Key Aspects:
1. Automated Teller Machines (ATMs): Withdraw cash, transfer funds.
2. Direct Deposit: Electronic transfer of salaries, benefits.
3. Debit Card Purchases: Immediate deduction from bank account.
4. Mobile Banking: Transactions via mobile devices.

slides.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of e-banking
content: Advantages:
- Convenience (24/7 access).
- Speed and efficiency.
- Reduces paper use.
Disadvantages:
- Security concerns (fraud, hacking).
- Limited capabilities compared to in-person services.
- Technology and power dependency.

slides.title: 5.7 Indigenous Financial Institutions
content: Ethiopia has traditional institutions like Iqub and Iddir.
Iqub (Saving Club):
- Rotating savings and credit association.
- Members contribute regularly, one member receives the total each cycle.
- Used for weddings, funerals, building houses.
Iddir (Funeral Association):
- Provides financial and material support for funerals.
- Members contribute monthly.

slides.title: Savings and Credit Cooperatives (SACCs)
content: SACCs: Semi-formal financial institutions.
They are outside the control of central authorities.
They have immense potential for financing short-term loans.
They support agricultural production technologies and income-generating activities.

slides.title: Features of Iqub and Iddir
content: Iqub:
- Based on social ties.
- Homogeneous groups.
- Low risk of default.
- Low administration costs.
Iddir:
- Found everywhere in Ethiopia.
- Provides financial and material assistance.
- Has by-laws and powerful social sanctions.
- Most funds are deposited in banks.

slides.title: Unit 6: Economic Growth
content: Economics is a social science about making decisions with scarce resources.
Microeconomics: Decisions at individual level.
Macroeconomics: Decisions at national level.
Macroeconomic Goals: Economic growth, low unemployment, price stability, balanced trade.

slides.title: 6.1 Review of Macroeconomic Variables
content: Current Account Balance: Exports (X) - Imports (M).
Trade Surplus: X > M (desirable).
Trade Deficit: X < M (not desirable).
Inflation: Increase in the general price level.
Cost-push inflation: Caused by high production costs.
Demand-pull inflation: Caused by high demand.

slides.title: Other Macroeconomic Variables
content: Economic Growth: Increase in output (GDP).
Very desirable for raising living standards.
Unemployment: People willing and able to work but without jobs.
Types of Unemployment:
- Frictional (job search).
- Structural (decline of an industry).
- Seasonal (time of year).
- Cyclical (economic recession).

sections.section_title: Definition and Measurement of Economic Growth

slides.title: 6.2 Definition and Measurement of Economic Growth
content: Short-run Economic Growth: Increase in Real GDP (RGDP).
Growth Rate (g) = [(RGDPt - RGDPt-1) / RGDPt-1] × 100%
Long-run Economic Growth: Sustained increase in per capita RGDP and structural change.
Per Capita RGDP = RGDP / Population.
Structural change: Shift from agriculture to industry (industrialization).

slides.title: Economic Growth vs Economic Development
content: Economic Growth: Quantitative increase in GDP or per capita income.
Economic Development: Broader concept involving social, political, and economic transformation.
Growth can occur without development.
Development requires growth but is not guaranteed by it.
Growth is a subset of development.

slides.title: 6.3 Sources of Economic Growth
content: Differences in living standards are due to differences in Productivity.
Productivity: Output per worker.
Productivity determines income and standard of living.

slides.title: Determinants of Productivity
content: 1. Physical Capital per worker: Tools and machinery.
2. Human Capital per worker: Knowledge and skills from education and training.
3. Natural Resources per worker: Land, water, minerals.
4. Technological Knowledge: Best ways to produce goods and services.
Example: A farmer with a tractor (more physical capital) is more productive than one with an ox.

slides.title: Characteristics of Modern Economic Growth
content: Simon Kuznets identified five characteristics:
1. High rates of increase in per capita income.
2. High rates of increase in factor productivity.
3. High rates of structural transformation (shift from agriculture to industry).
4. Increase in rates of saving and investment.
5. Increasing application of modern scientific knowledge in production.

slides.title: Classification of Countries by Income
content: World Bank Classification (by GNI per capita):
1. Low-Income Countries (LICs): $975 or less.
2. Lower Middle-Income Countries (LMCs): $976 - $3,855.
3. Upper Middle-Income Countries (UMCs): $3,856 - $11,906.
4. High-Income Countries: $11,907 or more.
Least Developed Countries (LDCs): 49 countries (33 in Africa, 15 in Asia, + Haiti) with low income, low human capital, and high vulnerability.

sections.section_title: The Weaknesses of Using GDP / GDP Per Capita

slides.title: 6.4 Weaknesses of GDP / GDP Per Capita
content: GDP measures total income and expenditure but is not a perfect measure of well-being.
Limitations:
- Excludes Leisure (work longer, GDP rises, but well-being may fall).
- Excludes Non-market Activities (household production, volunteer work).
- Excludes Quality of the Environment (pollution).
- Excludes Income Distribution (inequality).
- Excludes Underground Economy (black market).

sections.section_title: The Business Cycle and Its Phases

slides.title: 6.5 The Business Cycle
content: Business Cycle: Irregular and unpredictable fluctuations in economic activity.
Measured by GDP, employment, and income.
Phases of the Business Cycle:
1. Prosperity (Boom/Peak): High demand, high employment, high prices.
2. Recession: Economic slowdown, falling demand and employment.
3. Depression (Slump/Trough): Lowest point of economic activity.
4. Recovery (Expansion): Economy rebounds, output and employment rise.

slides.title: Business Cycle Diagram
content: The business cycle shows actual RGDP fluctuating around the trend line (potential RGDP).
Peak: Highest point of a cycle.
Trough: Lowest point of a cycle.
The cycle is irregular, not regular or predictable.
Policy goals: Minimize fluctuations, maintain long-run growth.

presentation_slides.unit_title: An Overview of the Ethiopian Economy

slides.title: Unit 7: The Ethiopian Economy
content: Ethiopian economy has changed from market-oriented to centrally planned and back to market-oriented.
Pre-1974: Feudal system, agriculture based.
1974-1991: Socialist/Command economy.
1991-Present: Market-oriented economy.
Key sectors: Agriculture, Industry, Services.

slides.title: 7.1 Components of GDP
content: GDP (Y) is divided into four components for analysis:
Y = C + I + G + NX
Where:
C = Consumption
I = Investment
G = Government Purchases
NX = Net Exports (Exports - Imports)

slides.title: Components of GDP: Definitions
content: Consumption (C): Spending by households on goods and services (except new housing).
Includes: Durable goods (cars, appliances), Nondurable goods (food, clothing), Services (healthcare, education).
Investment (I): Spending on capital goods used in future production.
Includes: Machinery, equipment, structures, new housing, inventory.
Note: Investment in economics is not financial investment (stocks/bonds).

slides.title: Government Purchases and Net Exports
content: Government Purchases (G): Spending by all levels of government on goods and services.
Includes: Salaries of government employees, public works.
Excludes: Transfer payments (social security, unemployment benefits).
Net Exports (NX): Exports - Imports.
NX = X - M.
Imports are subtracted because they are included in C, I, or G but are produced abroad.

slides.title: 7.2 Real GDP Vs Nominal GDP
content: Nominal GDP: GDP valued at current-year prices.
Real GDP: GDP valued at constant (base-year) prices.
Real GDP removes the effect of price changes and measures changes in output.
Real GDP is a better measure of economic growth.

slides.title: GDP Deflator
content: GDP Deflator: A measure of the overall price level.
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100
In the base year, GDP Deflator = 100.
Inflation Rate = [(GDP Deflator in year 2 - GDP Deflator in year 1) / GDP Deflator in year 1] × 100%
Example: If GDP Deflator rises from 100 to 171, inflation rate is 71%.

slides.title: Numerical Example: Real and Nominal GDP
content: Year 2010 (Base Year):
Nominal GDP = 27,500, Real GDP = 27,500, Deflator = 100
Year 2011:
Nominal GDP = 62,000, Real GDP = 47,500, Deflator = 131
Year 2012:
Nominal GDP = 100,000, Real GDP = 67,500, Deflator = 148

sections.section_title: The Agricultural Sector in the Ethiopian Economy

slides.title: 7.3 The Agricultural Sector
content: Agriculture is the backbone of the Ethiopian economy.
It contributes 33-45% of GDP, 80% of exports, and employs 85% of the population.
Major products: Crops (food crops, cash crops), Livestock.
Problems: Drought, soil degradation, land fragmentation, poor marketing, lack of technology.

slides.title: Roles of the Agricultural Sector
content: 1. Source of food and raw materials.
- Backward linkages: Demand for industrial inputs.
- Forward linkages: Supplies raw materials, reduces cost of living for urban areas.
2. Source of capital: Through taxes, terms of trade, and compulsory delivery.
3. Contribution to GDP.
4. Contribution to employment (85% of population).

slides.title: Structure of the Agricultural Sector
content: 1. Smallholder Farming System:
- Dominant (90% of production, 95% of crop area).
- Mixed farming, household size ~5 members, average land < 2 hectares.
2. Pastoral/Nomadic System:
- Livestock-based, in lowland areas (~40% of land).
- Supports ~5.5 million people.
3. Commercial Farming System:
- Large-scale farms (state farms and private).
- Produces cotton, coffee, sugarcane, etc.
- Inefficient but strategic.

sections.section_title: The Industrial Sector in the Ethiopian Economy

slides.title: 7.4 The Industrial Sector
content: Small but growing, contributes ~13% of GDP and ~9.5% of employment.
Dominant sub-sectors: Manufacturing (38%), Construction (25%), Electric and Water supply (18%).
Products: Textiles, foodstuffs, beverages, cement, leather, etc.

slides.title: Roles of the Industrial Sector
content: 1. Output Contribution:
- Food and beverages dominate (48% of gross value).
2. Employment Contribution:
- Food and beverage (50%), Non-metal (14%), Paper and printing (10.9%) are the largest employers.
3. Foreign Exchange Contribution:
- Textiles contribute the most (41.5%), followed by food and beverages (32.9%).
- Opportunities through AGOA.

slides.title: Challenges in the Industrial Sector
content: Low industrial base.
Low productivity and underutilization of capacity.
Shortage of foreign exchange and raw materials.
Heavy dependence on imported technology.
Low skills and management.
Opportunities: AGOA and European market access.

sections.section_title: The Service Sector in the Ethiopian Economy

slides.title: 7.5 The Service Sector
content: The service sector produces intangible goods.
Includes: Trade, hotels, transport, communication, banking, insurance, education, health, government services.
Share in GDP has grown significantly (~45-46%), now rivaling agriculture.

slides.title: Roles of the Service Sector
content: 1. Output Contribution: Large share in GDP.
2. Employment Contribution: Second largest sector after agriculture.
- Creating permanent jobs through private investment and infrastructure.
3. Foreign Exchange Earnings:
- Services from Ethiopian Airlines, Shipping Lines, Tourism, etc.
- In 2008/09, service exports reached nearly 2 billion dollars.

slides.title: Components of the Service Sector
content: Distributive Services: Trade, hotels, restaurants, transport, communication.
Other Services: Education, health, banking, insurance, public administration.
GDP share of services increased from 41.1% in 2002/03 to 46% in 2009/10.
Activities can be physical (repair, cooking), intellectual (education), or aesthetic (art, music).

slides.title: 7.6 Agriculture vs Industrial Development
content: Traditional view: Industry as the leading sector.
Ethiopian Strategy: Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI).
ADLI views agriculture as the leading and dynamic sector.
Argues that without agricultural development, industrial growth will be weak.
The agricultural sector must be developed to supply food and raw materials for industry.

slides.title: ADLI Strategy Rationale
content: ADLI focuses on:
- Improving agricultural productivity.
- Creating backward and forward linkages.
- Generating surplus for investment in other sectors.
- Providing raw materials and cheap food for the industrial labor force.
Debate: Some argue for prioritizing industry for faster growth.
Evaluation: ADLI is the current approach, emphasizing agriculture's foundational role.

slides.title: Unit 8: Business Startups and Innovation
content: Innovation is a critical element for business growth.
It involves creating new ideas and implementing them.
This unit covers types of innovation, business startups, types of business organizations, and feasibility analysis.

slides.title: 8.1 Innovation
content: Innovation: A new or improved product, process, or method that creates value.
Two key elements: Creativity + Implementation.
Types of Innovation:
1. Organizational
2. Process
3. Product
4. Marketing
5. Eco-Innovation

slides.title: Types of Innovation
content: Product Innovation: Introduction of a new or improved good or service (e.g., electric vehicles).
Process Innovation: New production/delivery methods (e.g., SaaS technology).
Marketing Innovation: New marketing strategies (e.g., Haagen Dazs's waste-free container).
Organizational Innovation: New business practices (e.g., 4-day workweek).
Eco-Innovation: Innovation that contributes to environmental sustainability (e.g., cold-water detergents).

slides.title: Creative Destruction
content: Concept by Joseph Schumpeter.
Innovation destroys old business models and technologies.
Products become obsolete, companies close, people become unemployed.
But this leads to new solutions, industries, and higher quality of life.
Examples: Nokia (failed to innovate), Uber (disrupted taxi industry).

slides.title: Famous Innovators
content: Steve Jobs (Smartphone with iPad).
Marie Curie (Radioactivity).
Elon Musk (Electric cars).
Thomas Edison (Electric light bulb).
Alexander Graham Bell (Telephone).
Leonardo DaVinci (Parachute).
Innovation is key to survival and growth.

slides.title: 8.2 Business Startups
content: Business Startup: A company in its early stages, designed for rapid growth.
Focus: High revenue and growth potential.
Goal: To create a scalable product or service.
Often not profitable initially, funding comes from investors.

slides.title: Startups vs Small Businesses
content: Startups:
- Focus on rapid growth and market share.
- Seek significant funding (venture capital, angel investors).
- High risk, high return.
- Examples: Uber, Tesla.
Small Businesses:
- Operate in a local or niche market.
- Stable, sustainable operations.
- Profit-focused from the start.
- Examples: Local grocery store, bakery.

slides.title: Startup Funding
content: Seed Funding: Early-stage financing to support product development.
Angel Investors: Wealthy individuals who invest in startups.
Venture Capital: Professional investors managing funds for startups.
Funding is essential for startups to cover R&D and scaling costs.

slides.title: 8.3 Types of Business Organizations
content: Three main forms:
1. Sole Proprietorship
2. Partnership
3. Corporation
Each has different ownership, liability, and management structures.

slides.title: Sole Proprietorship
content: Owned by a single individual.
Characteristics: Single ownership, no separation of ownership and management, unlimited liability.
Advantages: Easiest to start, flexibility, maximum authority, personal touch.
Disadvantages: Limited resources, unlimited liability, lack of continuity.

slides.title: Partnership
content: Owned by two or more persons.
Characteristics: Agreement, sharing of profits, unlimited liability for general partners.
Advantages: Easy to form, larger resources, better decisions, shared risk.
Disadvantages: Unlimited liability, instability, limited capital, potential conflicts.

slides.title: Corporation
content: A separate legal entity owned by shareholders.
Characteristics: Limited liability, shares represent ownership.
Managed by a board of directors elected by shareholders.
Advantages: Limited liability, easy transfer of shares, ability to raise large capital.
Disadvantages: Double taxation, complex formation, less personal control.

slides.title: 8.4 Business Feasibility Analysis
content: Feasibility Study: A preliminary assessment to determine if a business idea is viable.
Proof of Business Concept: Demonstrates if a project is feasible before a business plan.
It is less expensive and faster than a business plan.
Answers: Will it work? Is it profitable? Should we proceed?

slides.title: Feasibility Study vs Business Plan
content: Feasibility Study:
- Quick and general.
- Shows viability.
- Saves time and money.
Business Plan:
- Detailed road map.
- Includes timelines, budgets, staffing.
- Used for investment/funding and management blueprint.

slides.title: Developing a Feasibility Study
content: 1. Business Idea: Describe the concept clearly.
2. Key People: Profiles and skills of the team.
3. Personal Objectives: What do you want to achieve?
4. The Market: Customers, segments, competition.
5. Business Overview: Location, advantages/disadvantages.

slides.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA)
content: CBA is a process of weighing the total expected costs against the total expected benefits.
It helps decide if a course of action is financially sound.
Benefit-Cost Ratio = Total Benefits / Total Costs.
If B/C ratio > 1, the project is worthwhile.
Consider both tangible and intangible costs and benefits.

slides.title: Steps in Cost-Benefit Analysis
content: Step 1: Compile lists of all costs and benefits.
Step 2: Give the costs and benefits a monetary value.
Step 3: Add up total costs and total benefits.
Step 4: Calculate the B/C ratio.
Step 5: Interpret the result.
If B/C > 1, proceed with the decision.
If B/C < 1, reconsider the action.

slides.title: SWOT Analysis
content: A tool used in feasibility studies and business plans.
SWOT stands for:
Strengths: Internal positive attributes.
Weaknesses: Internal negative attributes.
Opportunities: External positive factors.
Threats: External negative factors.
Helps in strategic planning and decision-making.
